question: Marlow reports EBITDA of £150m. That includes a £12m one-off restructuring charge and a £5m gain on selling a warehouse. Peers trade at a median of 11× EBITDA. What EBITDA should you apply the multiple to, and what enterprise value does it give?
model_answer_md:
**Normalise first**, so the multiple prices recurring profit.

- Add back the one-off restructuring charge: +£12m
- Remove the one-off gain on the warehouse: −£5m

$$\text{Normalised EBITDA} = £150\text{m} + £12\text{m} - £5\text{m} = \mathbf{£157\text{m}}$$

$$\text{EV} = 11 \times £157\text{m} = \mathbf{£1{,}727\text{m}}$$

Against £1,650m on the reported figure, that is **£77m** more value from £7m of EBITDA — which is exactly why buyers scrutinise every adjustment. Peers' EBITDA must be cleaned the same way, or the comparison is inconsistent.
key_points: Add back one-off charges; remove one-off gains
Each £1m of adjustment is worth £11m at this multiple — scrutinise them
Normalise the peers on the same basis

follow_ups.question: When would you challenge a 'one-off' add-back?
follow_ups.answer_md: When it recurs. A company that books 'restructuring' every year has a recurring cost, and adding it back flatters EBITDA. I would look at several years of adjustments and treat anything regular as part of the business.

follow_ups.question: Is the warehouse gain in EBITDA in the first place?
follow_ups.answer_md: It depends on how the company presents it — some put disposal gains in operating profit, some below it. If it is inside reported EBITDA it must come out, because selling a warehouse is not a recurring operating activity.

weak_answer_note: Applying the multiple to reported EBITDA without adjusting, or adding back the gain instead of removing it.
